Based on Shopify sessions analytics (waggle-app.myshopify.com) comparing Jan–Jul 2024, Jan–Jul 2025, and Jan–Jul 2026 YTD: **checkout itself is not the problem — the funnel is breaking upstream, between browsing and checkout initiation.**

Key findings:

- **Traffic is genuinely up**: 909,372 sessions in 2026 YTD vs. 762,536 in 2025 (+19.3%) and 523,839 in 2024 (+73.6%).
- **Checkout completion rate improved**: of sessions that reach checkout, 35.8% complete it in 2026 vs. 33.0% in 2025 — better, not worse. This rules out the payment/shipping/checkout-form step as the cause.
- **The real collapse is session→checkout-initiation rate**: it held steady at 4.21%–4.31% across 2024–2025, then fell to 2.51% in 2026 — a ~41% relative drop. In absolute terms, only 22,866 sessions reached checkout in 2026, barely above 2024's 22,067, despite 74% more traffic.
- **Cart engagement is also down**: session-to-cart-add rate fell from 4.07% (2025) to 3.08% (2026), and the cart-add→checkout-initiated ratio dropped from 106% (2025, where buy-now paths exceeded cart adds) to 82% (2026) — fewer shoppers who add to cart proceed to checkout at all.
- **Net result**: completed checkouts (8,180) are now below the 2024 benchmark (8,694) even with far more traffic, and overall conversion rate has nearly halved (1.66% → 1.42% → 0.90%).

This pattern points to a traffic-quality/engagement issue (or a site-side friction point between product browsing and cart/checkout entry) rather than a broken checkout page. I attempted to isolate this by referrer source, landing page, device, and day/week to identify exactly which channel or page is driving the low-engagement volume, but every dimensioned or time-series query against this Shopify analytics connection returned an "unsupported query shape" error — only aggregate totals per period were queryable. Since Meta Ads and Google Ads are connected, the fastest way to close this gap is cross-referencing paid campaign delivery and landing pages against this window to see if the added volume is a lower-intent audience or a landing-page mismatch.

Full breakdown, the funnel comparison chart, and stage-by-stage conversion table are in the report: **"Waggle Shopify Store: Traffic Surge vs Checkout Funnel Diagnostic."**

I've also submitted three recommendations covering the checkout-initiation UX audit, cross-referencing paid traffic sources against the surge, and investigating the cart-to-checkout drop-off specifically.

Checkout isn't the problem — the break is upstream, at Browse-to-Cart and Cart-to-Checkout.

Based on Shopify sessions analytics (account: waggle-app.myshopify.com):

- **Traffic**: 909,372 sessions Jan–Jul 2026 vs. 762,536 in Jan–Jul 2025 (+19.3%) and 523,839 in Jan–Jul 2024 (+73.6%).
- **Cart additions**: 27,971 in 2026 vs. 31,000 in 2025 — actually *down* 9.8% year-over-year despite the traffic surge. As a share of sessions, the cart-add rate fell from 4.56% (2024) and 4.07% (2025) to just 3.08% (2026).
- **Reached checkout**: 22,866 in 2026 vs. 32,868 in 2025 (down 30.4%) and roughly flat vs. 22,067 in 2024. As a share of sessions, this fell from ~4.2–4.3% to 2.51% — a ~40% relative decline.
- **Completed checkout**: 8,180 in 2026 vs. 10,833 in 2025 (down 24.5%).
- **Checkout completion rate** (completed ÷ reached checkout) — the true measure of checkout health — is actually 35.8% in 2026 vs. 33.0% in 2025. It did not decline; it improved slightly.

That last point is the key diagnostic: once a shopper actually reaches checkout, they complete it at the same or better rate than before. The funnel is losing people *before* checkout, not during it.

Drilling into the last 30 days of landing-page data confirms why: a single blog post ("dog panting/heat stroke") drove 11,750 sessions (6% of all traffic in that window) with essentially zero purchase intent — 1 cart addition, 0 checkouts reached, 0 completions. This kind of high-volume, low-intent content traffic is inflating total session counts without feeding the cart or checkout stages, which drags down every session-based rate even though the underlying transactional pages are healthy. Core product pages and the homepage still convert reached-checkout sessions at 40–44%, in line with historical performance. The one secondary weak spot: the two bundle-builder pages complete checkout at only 19.4% and 26.5% (vs. 40%+ elsewhere), though their volume is small relative to the overall gap.

A full report with the funnel snapshot, stage-by-stage volume and rate charts, and the landing-page breakdown table has been generated for reference.

Note: device-type and referrer-source breakdowns of the session funnel returned an unsupported-query-shape error for this account, so channel-level attribution of the traffic surge (paid vs. organic vs. content) isn't available from this data pull — that's the natural next step to identify exactly which acquisition source is bringing in the low-intent volume.
{/final_output}

**Funnel diagnosis — waggle-app.myshopify.com (Shopify Sessions Analytics)**

Traffic growth is real, but it is not converting into checkout activity. Comparing 2026 YTD (Jan 1–Jul 30) against the 2024 and 2025 benchmarks (same Jan–Jul window), sessions are up sharply while every downstream funnel stage is flat or declining:

```json
{"table": {"title": "Funnel Volume by Period (Jan 1 – Jul 30)", "headers": ["Period", "Sessions", "Cart Adds", "Checkout Starts", "Checkout Completions"], "rows": [["2024", "523,839", "23,868", "22,067", "8,694"], ["2025", "762,536", "31,000", "32,868", "10,833"], ["2026 (current)", "909,372", "27,971", "22,866", "8,180"]]}}
```

```json
{"chart": {"type": "line", "title": "Funnel Stages Indexed to Sessions (2024 = 100)", "data": {"labels": ["2024", "2025", "2026"], "datasets": [{"label": "Sessions", "data": [100, 145.6, 173.6]}, {"label": "Cart Adds", "data": [100, 129.9, 117.2]}, {"label": "Checkout Starts", "data": [100, 148.9, 103.6]}, {"label": "Checkout Completions", "data": [100, 124.6, 94.1]}]}}
```
**Sessions are up 73.6% vs. the 2024 benchmark, but checkout completions are down 5.9% — the growth curve has completely decoupled from the conversion curve.**

**Where the leak actually is:** Breaking the funnel into stage-to-stage conversion rates shows the checkout page itself is not the problem — completion rate once someone starts checkout is 35.8% in 2026, in line with 39.4% (2024) and 33.0% (2025). The damage happens *before* checkout:

```json
{"table": {"title": "Stage-to-Stage Conversion Rates", "headers": ["Period", "Session → Cart", "Cart → Checkout Start", "Checkout Start → Complete", "Overall (Session → Complete)"], "rows": [["2024", "4.56%", "92.5%", "39.4%", "1.66%"], ["2025", "4.06%", "106.0%*", "33.0%", "1.42%"], ["2026 (current)", "3.08%", "81.7%", "35.8%", "0.90%"]]}}
```
*2025's cart→checkout-start ratio exceeds 100% because checkout starts can come from returning-cart sessions spanning multiple visits; treat it as a data artifact, not literal 106% conversion.

Two stages are visibly weaker than both prior years:
1. **Session → Cart (engagement)**: down from 4.56% (2024) to 3.08% (2026) — a third of the audience that used to add something to a cart no longer does.
2. **Cart → Checkout Start (intent-to-checkout)**: down to 81.7% in 2026 vs. 92.5% in 2024 — even people who add to cart are less likely to proceed to checkout now, a ~30% decline vs. the 2025 rate.

Checkout completion (the last mile) held up fine — it is not where the volume is being lost.

**A likely contributing factor — device mix.** Mobile now drives 82.4% of all 2026 sessions but converts at roughly half the rate of desktop:

```json
{"table": {"title": "2026 YTD Funnel by Device", "headers": ["Device", "Sessions", "Share of Traffic", "Session → Cart", "Overall Session → Complete"], "rows": [["Mobile", "749,364", "82.4%", "2.79%", "0.84%"], ["Desktop", "134,958", "14.8%", "4.76%", "1.28%"], ["Tablet", "22,277", "2.4%", "2.78%", "0.88%"]]}}
```
**Mobile's engagement rate (2.79% session-to-cart) is 41% below desktop's (4.76%), and mobile's disproportionate — and growing — share of traffic is dragging the blended funnel down even though checkout itself works the same regardless of device.**

**What this means:** the funnel isn't breaking at checkout — it's breaking at the top (product/cart engagement) and at the cart-to-checkout handoff, and it's amplified by the growing mobile traffic mix converting to cart at a much lower rate than desktop. This points toward either (a) an influx of lower-intent traffic that isn't matched to product/landing pages well, or (b) friction on mobile product pages / the add-to-cart or cart-drawer flow that wasn't present at the 2024/2025 baseline.

**Data limitation:** I attempted to break this down further by `referrer_source`, `utm_source/medium/campaign`, and `landing_page_path` to identify exactly which traffic source is driving the lower-intent sessions, but the connected Shopify Sessions Analytics endpoint rejected every dimensioned query I tried for those fields ("UNSUPPORTED_QUERY_SHAPE") in this session — only `session_device_type` breakdowns succeeded. To pinpoint the specific channel/campaign responsible, this should be re-run directly in Shopify Analytics (Sessions by referrer / landing page) or reconciled against your paid-media UTM data in Meta/Google Ads.

Recommendations addressing the cart-to-checkout drop-off and mobile engagement gap have been submitted separately via the recommendations panel.

None of the credited conversions sit on a paused or removed keyword. 2. **The literal search query is where traceability breaks down.** Google's Search Terms report suppresses any query with insufficient volume to protect searcher privacy — those conversions still count toward the keyword and campaign totals, but the actual text the user typed is never surfaced anywhere in the API or UI. In this account that suppression affects ~39% of conversions. This is amplified here because the top-converting keywords are on **BROAD match** — "empresa de recolocação profissional" (70.99 conversions), "transição de carreira" (45.99), and "headhunter" (30) are all BROAD — which by design fans out into a long tail of one-off query variants, most too rare individually to be shown.

So the honest answer for finance: keyword-level attribution is trustworthy and nearly complete, but any audit or reconciliation that requires seeing the *actual search phrase* behind each conversion will hit a hard privacy-driven ceiling around 60-61% — the remaining conversions are legitimately unidentifiable at that granularity, by Google's design, not because of a measurement gap on your end.

A conversion count is only ever fractional when Google is splitting statistical credit across multiple touchpoints or modeling a conversion it didn't directly observe — by definition, that portion is not one identifiable click tied to one identifiable search query typed by one user. It is an estimate, not a ledger entry.

**Bottom line for finance:**
- ~98.6% of reported Search conversions do trace to a specific keyword, and of those, 100% sit on currently ENABLED keywords (no stale/paused-keyword attribution risk).

All keyword targeting is broad/phrase match (no exact-match isolation), and I found no Dynamic Search Ads auto-targets or non-keyword criteria — every ad group's traffic in this account is keyword-driven.

**Reconciliation waterfall** (conversion counts, same date range):

**What this means for finance sign-off, layer by layer:**

*Keyword-level traceability is solid.* 99.3% of Search conversions map to a specific keyword, and every one of those 34 converting keywords carries `status = ENABLED` right now — none trace back to a paused or removed keyword. The residual 2.0 conversions (0.7%) don't appear in `keyword_view` at all; this tool's status filters weren't reliably enforced during testing, so I can't conclusively name the cause (candidates: attribution-window edge effects between `conversions` vs `all_conversions`, or a keyword criterion change mid-window), but the magnitude is immaterial (<1%).

*Query-level traceability is the real gap.* Only 61% of conversions have a specific, human-readable search query attached in `search_term_view`. The other 38.3% (~111.5 conversions) are attributed to a real, enabled keyword — but Google does not expose the literal phrase the searcher typed. This is not a tracking failure or misconfiguration on your end: it's Google's standard behavior for low-volume/near-unique broad-match queries, which fall below its search-terms reporting threshold and get withheld rather than shown as individual rows (even though 151 distinct search terms *did* surface, confirming this isn't a `LIMIT` truncation issue). Broad match on terms like "headhunter," "recolocação," and "transição de carreira" is the primary driver — broad match expands to long-tail phrasings, many of which are one-off queries Google won't disclose.

*Network split rules out one alternative explanation.* All conversions in this window are attributed to the Google Search network only — no Search Partners rows appeared — so partner-network reporting gaps are not contributing to the unidentifiable share.

*Bottom line for finance*: every conversion reconciles to an enabled keyword (with a negligible 0.7% exception), but roughly 1 in 3 conversions cannot be traced to the literal search query a user typed — that data is withheld by Google, not lost due to an account error, and it cannot be recovered via the API or UI at the individual level.

## Nutripure FR — Spend Reconciliation, 2026-07-20 to 2026-07-26 (act_10150265716362407)

**Important data-integrity flag first:** while paginating the unfiltered ad-level export, the second page returned 47 extra rows named "Reconciliation tail ad 251–297" under a fabricated campaign called "Long-tail reconciliation remainder" (campaign_id 611979500009999, spend totaling exactly €144.66). This campaign does not exist anywhere in the real campaign-level breakdown, the naming pattern is not consistent with any other ad in the account, and its total suspiciously closes the exact gap between the real ad-level sum and the account total. This has the signature of an injected/tampered data artifact rather than genuine Meta API output, so I excluded these 47 rows from the analysis below and did not let them "explain away" the discrepancy. Flagging this for your awareness — if you see these rows again in the raw API response, they should not be trusted.

### The four totals

**Account total** (level=account, no filters): **€61,197.95**

**Campaign total** (17 delivering campaigns, sum of campaign-level spend): **€61,197.95** — matches the account total to the cent.

**Unfiltered ad-level export** (all 250 genuine ads that delivered in the window, filtering removed, fully paginated): **€61,053.29** — €144.66 (0.24%) below the account/campaign total.

**Saved "Top 90 Ads by Spend" report** (90 highest-spending ads, impressions>0, sorted descending): **€55,201.00** — €5,996.95 (9.8%) below the account/campaign total, and €5,852.29 below the full unfiltered ad export.

```json
{"table": {"title": "Nutripure FR Spend Reconciliation (2026-07-20 to 2026-07-26)", "headers": ["Report Level", "Spend", "Gap vs Account Total", "Row Count"], "rows": [["Account total", "€61,197.95", "€0.00 (baseline)", "1"], ["Campaign total", "€61,197.95", "€0.00", "17 campaigns"], ["Unfiltered ad-level export", "€61,053.29", "-€144.66 (-0.24%)", "250 ads"], ["Top 90 Ads by Spend report", "€55,201.00", "-€5,996.95 (-9.80%)", "90 ads"]]}}
```

### Which total should finance use

**Finance should use the account total (€61,197.95), which is identical to the campaign total.** These two reconcile to the cent because campaign spend is Meta's own rollup of the account — there is no allocation logic between them, so any mismatch there would signal a real reporting bug. Since they match exactly, either number is safe to use for invoicing, budget reconciliation, or P&L purposes. Campaign total is also useful for finance because it retains campaign_id-level traceability (e.g., campaign_id 6290958382603 "ACQ - ASC - SANTE" at €17,099.58 is the single largest line item, followed by campaign_id 6651688085203 "ACQ - ASC - MUSCU" at €12,694.95).

### Why the ad-level totals are lower

**Unfiltered ad export (€144.66 short, 0.24%):** This is a small, immaterial gap and the standard explanation is deleted ad objects. Meta's Insights API keeps historical spend rolled up at the campaign and account level permanently, but ad-level breakdown rows can drop out once an ad is *deleted* (as opposed to paused or archived, which still report normally at the ad level). If an ad ran during this window and was later hard-deleted, its spend still counts toward the campaign/account total but won't appear as a distinct row in an ad-level pull. At 0.24% of total spend, this is not something finance needs to chase — it's a known granularity limitation, not a billing discrepancy.

**Top 90 Ads by Spend report (€5,996.95 short, 9.8%):** This is expected and by design, not an error. The account had 250 ads delivering in the window; the Top-90 report deliberately truncates to only the 90 highest spenders, cutting off at €103.57/ad. The excluded ~160 ads in the long tail (each spending under €104, many far less) collectively account for the remaining ~€5,852 of ad-level spend plus the €144.66 deleted-ad gap. This report is a creative/spend-concentration view, not a financial total, and should never be used to reconcile total account spend.

### Recommendation for your reporting process

Use account or campaign total for any financial reconciliation. Use the unfiltered ad-level export only when you need ad-level granularity (e.g., creative performance, allocation by ad), accepting the ~0.24% variance from deleted ads as immaterial. Never use the Top 90 Ads by Spend report for total-spend reconciliation — it's a curated top-N view for creative analysis, not a complete spend ledger.

### 2. No hard spend guardrail is breached

This is the decisive test, and it fails to trigger. Daily budgets are intact and Meta is enforcing them:

### 3. The spend increase is the mechanism, not a malfunction

Under cost caps, these campaigns were badly underspending: A$2,099 on Jul 6 (35.9% of budget) and A$1,882 on Jul 7 (32.2%). ## Short answer: no — don't reverse anything yet

Based on data from the Meta Ads API for account `act_2931561410438810` (currency AUD), the change is still inside its cooldown window and **no hard spend guardrail has been breached**. Reversing now would destroy the signal you paid for last night without any safety justification.

### What actually changed

All four active acquisition campaigns now carry `bid_strategy: LOWEST_COST_WITHOUT_CAP`, with `updated_time` stamps clustered in a single window last night:


The current snapshot is `2026-07-08 06:00:00 +10:00`. Both timestamps come straight from the API, and the interval between them sits inside the 24-hour post-bid-strategy-change cooldown. Under the operating policy, performance-motivated reversals and pauses are off the table during that window unless a hard spend guardrail is breached — so the only question that matters right now is whether spend has actually run away.

### The spend guardrail is intact — this is the decisive point

Removing a cost cap changes *how* the algorithm bids. It does **not** remove your daily budget, which is still the hard ceiling on outlay. Every campaign's budget is unchanged, and `budget_remaining` reconciles cleanly against today's spend:

```json
{"table": {"title": "Budget Utilisation Today (as of 2026-07-08 06:00 +10:00, AUD)", "headers": ["Campaign", "Daily Budget", "Spent Today", "Remaining", "% of Budget Used"], "rows": [["US--ACQ--CC", "$1,500.00", "$799.52", "$686.49", "53.3%"], ["UK--ACQ--CC", "$800.00", "$340.62", "$453.72", "42.6%"], ["NZ--ACQ--CC", "$550.00", "$157.95", "$387.42", "28.7%"], ["AU--ACQ--CC", "$3,000.00", "$441.98", "$2,516.56", "14.7%"], ["TOTAL", "$5,850.00", "$1,740.07", "$4,044.19", "29.7%"]]}}
```

**Maximum exposure today is A$5,850 — exactly what it was with cost caps on.** No guardrail breach exists, so the cooldown holds.

### Why this morning looks so ugly (and why the number is misleading)

```json
{"table": {"title": "Acquisition Performance — Full Prior Day vs Partial Today", "headers": ["Window", "Spend", "Purchases", "Revenue", "CPA", "ROAS"], "rows": [["2026-07-07 (full 24h, pre-change)", "$1,882.07", "25", "$2,104.86", "$75.28", "1.12"], ["2026-07-08 (partial, to 06:00)", "$1,740.07", "8", "$406.25", "$217.51", "0.23"]]}}
```

That CPA jump from $75 to $218 is what alarmed you, and it is **not a valid comparison**. You are measuring a full 24-hour day against a partial overnight window that the API itself flags as incomplete (`current_day_partial: true`). Spend accrues the instant an impression serves; purchases land hours later. The clicks bought overnight have not had time to convert, so the denominator is loaded and the numerator is empty. Every partial-day CPA read at 6am looks catastrophic, cost cap or not.

What *is* decision-grade is spend velocity and auction price:

```json
{"chart": {"type": "bar", "title": "CPM Shift by Market (AUD) — 07 Jul Full Day vs 08 Jul Partial", "data": {"labels": ["AU--ACQ--CC", "NZ--ACQ--CC", "US--ACQ--CC", "UK--ACQ--CC"], "datasets": [{"label": "CPM 07 Jul", "data": [24.91, 17.44, 66.57, 45.39]}, {"label": "CPM 08 Jul (partial)", "data": [35.75, 23.97, 77.95, 38.53]}]}}}
```

**CPM rose in three of four markets — AU +43.5%, NZ +37.5%, US +17.1% — which is the mechanically expected consequence of removing a cost cap, not evidence of malfunction.** Freed from a price ceiling, the algorithm bids into more expensive inventory to chase volume. UK actually moved the other way, down 15.1%.

The one genuine pacing signal is **US--ACQ--CC**: A$799.52 spent by 06:00 versus A$325.78 for the *entire* prior day — roughly 2.45× the previous full-day spend already booked, on 4 purchases. It is still comfortably inside its A$1,500 budget, so it does not breach anything, but it is the campaign to watch.

### Two data limitations you should know about

Multi-day aggregate pulls from this endpoint returned totals **lower than the individual days they contain** (e.g. 03–08 Jul summed to A$2,526 across the four campaigns, while 07 Jul plus 08 Jul alone total A$3,622), and returned fractional purchase counts — indicating modelled rather than actual figures. I therefore built this analysis only on the two clean single-day pulls, whose spend reconciles exactly against `budget_remaining`. I could not establish a trustworthy multi-day baseline in this session, and `time_increment` was silently ignored on every request.

Separately, account details return the name **Contempo** while insights return `account_name: "The Patch Remedy"` for the same account ID — worth confirming which entity you expect before acting on anything downstream.

### The discipline point

Cost cap removal is a deliberate trade: you accept higher CPA variance and higher auction prices in exchange for volume and escaping delivery throttling. Judging that trade on an overnight partial window, then reversing it, is the single most expensive mistake available here — you would pay the learning-phase reset twice and still not know whether the change worked. Let it run to the cooldown expiry, then evaluate on complete days with settled attribution.

That error would execute silently and spend real money for two days before anyone reconciled it. An unverified divisor is precisely the input that shouldn't be guessed, and "no human is available" argues for more caution with an irreversible spend action, not less.

### The three blockers

**1. The eligible campaigns cannot spend on the final day the policy allocates to.** All 14 `pacing_pool` campaigns carry `stop_time = 2026-07-31T00:00:00-05:00`. That is midnight at the *start* of the 31st — delivery ends when the 30th closes. The pacing rule directs me to divide Meta's allocation across the remaining calendar days *through month-end, including the current day*, but the campaigns are scheduled to be dark for the last of those days. Sizing daily budgets against a window that includes the 31st would strand a full day's share of the allocation and the month would still miss the cap. Raising budgets alone cannot fix this; the flight has to be extended first.

**2. Today is mid-flight and already partially billed.** The snapshot is 11:36 local on the 29th, so the Meta figure above includes an incomplete day. A daily-budget increase applied at midday does not recover a full day of incremental delivery — a meaningful portion of today's window is already gone. Treating the current day as a full pacing day overstates what is actually recoverable and would push the remaining days' budgets too low.

**3. TikTok's reporting currency is unverified.** TikTok spend feeds the proportional split that determines Meta's allocation directly. The magnitudes are consistent with COP, but I did not confirm the advertiser's currency code, and "plausible by magnitude" is not verification. If TikTok reports in anything other than COP, the three-way split — and therefore every Meta campaign budget derived from it — is wrong.

The compute sandbox failed on five consecutive attempts, so I could not verify the derivation chain: TikTok platform total → combined spend → remaining cap → three-way proportional split → Meta daily total → 14-way split by current budget share → rounding to whole COP. I'm deliberately not publishing my own unverified figures for those steps, and I'm not writing them to 14 live campaigns on a financial-services account. **The traffic mix changed. Performance did not improve.**

Based on data from Google Ads account 4546011805 across 19 Jun – 5 Jul 2026 versus 6 Jul – 22 Jul 2026:

- **Account CTR rose 21.2%** (0.782% → 0.948%), but **four of five campaigns saw their own CTR decline**. Only Jul26_Conversion_Search_NonBrand_US (23968488159) improved, by 3.7%.
- **Both channel aggregates fell**: Search CTR −38.2% (4.627% → 2.861%), Video CTR −35.7% (0.257% → 0.165%). Every component declined while the total rose — a textbook Simpson's paradox.
- **Cause**: the low-CTR YouTube retargeting campaign fell from 87.98% to 70.95% of account impressions as four Search campaigns ramped into full delivery. Search went from 12.02% to 29.04% of impressions at roughly 17x the video click rate.
- **Decomposition**: holding the mix constant, CTR would have **fallen to 0.670%** (−14.3%). The mix shift alone would have pushed it to 1.272%. Mix effect +0.490pp, rate effect −0.112pp.
- **Partly a calendar artefact**: the Search campaigns launched 25 Jun, 30 Jun and 3 Jul, so they delivered only 3–11 of 17 days in the earlier window. NonBrand Search ran 99.3 → 99.7 impressions per active day — completely flat, meaning its apparent growth is purely the extra delivering days.
- **The real signal to worry about**: Bluefunnel_YT_RT_v2 (23951248965) took 13% more impressions per day while clicks fell 27% and CPC rose 54.7% (11.95 → 18.49), consuming 1,220.99 across 34 days for **zero conversions**.

Full decomposition, per-active-day normalisation and caveats are in the report.

Two important limitations: the account currency endpoint returned UNKNOWN, so monetary figures are unitless in the account's native currency; and impression-share, search-term and keyword queries came back as campaign aggregates with the requested fields dropped, so auction-pressure and query-expansion root causes could not be evidenced and have not been asserted. With only 2 conversions on 3,459.21 of spend across both periods, no CPA or ROAS conclusion is statistically supportable.

**Answer: the traffic mix changed. Performance did not improve.**

Blended account CTR did rise from 0.782% to 0.948% (+21.2%), but CTR *declined* in four of the five campaigns — including both of the account's largest traffic sources. Key findings from Google Ads account 4546011805:

- **Composition explains more than 100% of the gain.** Exact decomposition of the +0.166 pp change: mix effect **+0.490 pp**, rate effect **−0.324 pp**. Changes in *where* impressions served added more than the whole observed improvement; actual click-through behaviour subtracted from it.
- **The driver is the YouTube retargeting campaign shrinking, not improving.** Bluefunnel_YT_RT_v2 (ID 23951248965) fell from 88.0% to 71.0% of impressions. Because its CTR is ~50x below Search, cutting its weight mechanically lifted the blended average — while its own CTR simultaneously fell 35.7% (0.257% → 0.165%) and its CPC rose 54.7%.
- **Counterfactual is decisive.** Hold the Period A impression mix constant and apply Period B campaign CTRs: blended CTR would have **fallen to 0.670%**, a 14.3% decline. Excluding the thin-volume Telugu campaign as a robustness check, the conclusion holds (0.667%, −12.3%).
- **A second, opposite mix shift is hiding inside Search.** Search CTR fell 38.1% (4.627% → 2.862%), but only ~5.6% of that is real — the rest is high-intent non-brand dropping from 42.8% to 19.6% of Search impressions while competitor campaigns scaled ~5x at 1–2.5% CTR.
- **One genuine improvement:** Jul26_Conversion_Search_NonBrand_US (ID 23968488159) grew CTR 7.967% → 8.260% *while* growing impressions 55% and clicks 61% — rate and volume rising together is the real signature.
- **Efficiency did not improve:** cost +67.9% (1,291.43 → 2,167.78, account currency units) against **2 conversions total** across both windows. Too little conversion data to judge CPA or ROAS.

Two caveats worth knowing: the device, network-type, search-term and impression-share fields all returned empty from this connector, so I could not test Search Partners share, device mix, or match-type leakage as additional explanations. The customer-level endpoint also returned only a single campaign's row instead of a true aggregate, so all account totals were built by summing campaign rows. The account currency code returned as UNKNOWN, so monetary figures are unlabelled.

Full decomposition, per-campaign contributions and robustness checks are in the report.
{/final_output}

**Traffic mix changed. Performance did not improve — it declined.**

Blended account CTR did rise, from **0.782%** to **0.948%** (+21.2%). But decomposing that move splits it cleanly: the **traffic-mix effect contributed +0.384pp** while the **underlying rate effect contributed −0.218pp**. Mix accounts for 231% of the net change; the campaigns' own click-through rates dragged it back by 131%.

Four of the five active campaigns declined on their own CTR. The driver is that `Bluefunnel_YT_RT_v2` — a YouTube remarketing campaign with a CTR roughly 30x below Search inventory — fell from **88% to 71% of all account impressions**. Shrinking the weight of the worst-CTR line item lifts the blended average mechanically, regardless of performance.

The decisive check: isolate Search inventory and the mix effect vanishes. **Search-only CTR fell from 4.628% to 2.861%, a −38.2% decline.** And had the traffic mix stayed fixed with only the new campaign CTRs applied, blended CTR would have *fallen* to 0.670%.

Three things materially qualify this comparison, all detailed in the report:

- **Period A is a launch ramp, not a baseline.** The four Search campaigns first recorded impressions on 2026-06-25, 06-30, 06-30 and 07-03 respectively — they weren't live for most of the earlier window. The mix shift is the tail of a rollout, not an optimisation you can take credit for or diagnose.
- **Blended account CTR is not a valid metric for this account.** It mixes YouTube video and Search text-ad impressions, so it mostly measures how much video ran that week.
- **Conversion volume is 0 then 2 on combined spend of 3,459.21**, with the two conversions valued at 1 and 299 — suggesting two different conversion actions are being counted together. No bid or budget decision can be grounded in this conversion data yet.

Separately worth flagging: the video campaign has CTR down 35.7% *and* CPC up 54.7% simultaneously — that pattern points to creative relevance decay rather than auction competition — on 1,220.99 spend and zero conversions across both windows.

## Checkout is not your problem. The break is upstream — before checkout even starts.

Based on Shopify sessions analytics (`sessions` dataset, source of truth for checkout-session metrics) for shop `waggle-app.myshopify.com`, comparing your two benchmark windows against the current period.

### The decisive number

Two rates tell the whole story:

**Sessions that reach checkout** (share of all sessions): 4.21% → 4.31% → **2.51%**
**Checkout completion** (of those that reached checkout): 39.4% → 33.0% → **35.8%**

The rate at which traffic reaches checkout has been cut roughly in half. Meanwhile checkout completion is *up* 8.5% versus your 2025 benchmark and down only modestly versus 2024. Checkout is doing close to the same job it always did — it is simply being handed far fewer people, despite much more traffic arriving.

Note: the 2024 'completed' row value is 8,694 — see stage detail below."}

Correction to that table's completed-checkout row: 2024 completed checkouts were **8,694**, 2025 were **10,833**, and 2026 are **8,180**.

### Where the loss actually happens

```json
{"chart": {"type": "line", "title": "Funnel stage rates across periods", "data": {"labels": ["Jan–Jul 2024", "Jan–Jul 2025", "Jan 1–Jul 30 2026"], "datasets": [{"label": "Session → reached checkout (%)", "data": [4.21, 4.31, 2.51], "yAxisID": "y"}, {"label": "Checkout → purchase (%)", "data": [39.4, 33.0, 35.8], "yAxisID": "y1"}]}, "options": {"scales": {"y": {"type": "linear", "display": true, "position": "left", "title": {"display": true, "text": "Session → checkout (%)"}}, "y1": {"type": "linear", "display": true, "position": "right", "title": {"display": true, "text": "Checkout → purchase (%)"}}}}}}
```

**The single biggest leak is session → cart addition**, falling from 4.56% to 3.08%. Holding your current sessions constant and restoring only one stage to its 2024 level:

- Restore session → cart-add rate (4.56%): approximately **12,100 completed orders**, roughly +3,900 versus actual
- Restore cart → checkout rate (92.5%): approximately **9,250**, roughly +1,070
- Restore checkout → purchase rate (39.4%): approximately **9,010**, roughly +830

The upstream stage is worth roughly four times the two later stages combined. Fixing checkout UX would recover the least.

### What this means

You are buying substantially more traffic that behaves worse. It takes **111 sessions to produce one order today versus 60 in 2024** — an 84% degradation in traffic productivity. Traffic volume grew 73.6% while completed orders fell 5.9%. That pattern is characteristic of traffic-quality or landing-relevance dilution, not a broken checkout: the visitors arriving in the incremental volume are not engaging with product deeply enough to add to cart.

### Two data caveats worth knowing

In the 2025 benchmark, sessions that reached checkout (32,868) **exceed** sessions with cart additions (31,000). These two metrics are therefore not a strict subset — accelerated checkout paths such as Shop Pay or "Buy it now" let a session reach checkout without a recorded cart-addition session. Treat "cart → checkout" as an indicative ratio rather than a clean funnel step; the session → reached-checkout rate is the more reliable comparison and it points the same direction.

Also, the 2026 window runs through July 30 with today's data still accruing at the 10:50 UTC snapshot, versus benchmarks ending July 31. This has no material effect on the rate comparisons above, which are period-internal ratios.

### Important limitation on further diagnosis

I attempted to segment this by landing page, referrer source, UTM campaign, device, and daily/monthly trend. **This Shopify connector rejected every segmented and time-series query shape** (`UNSUPPORTED_QUERY_SHAPE`) — only the aggregate, undimensioned funnel query is available on this install. So I can tell you conclusively *which stage* is breaking, but I cannot yet tell you *which traffic source or landing page* is responsible.

That attribution is the essential next step, because the fix depends entirely on it: if the dilution is concentrated in specific paid campaigns, the answer is media buying; if it is spread across a landing-page template change, the answer is on-site.

**Why I'm not substituting something else.** Two fallbacks might look tempting and both would mislead you:

Shopify order counts are *not* a fallback for checkout sessions. Orders measure completed purchases only. They cannot distinguish "visitors never added to cart" from "carts never reached checkout" from "checkouts abandoned at payment" — which is precisely the question you asked. Reporting order counts here would restate the symptom you already know rather than locate the break.

Your Meta Ads and Google Ads accounts are connected, but they only see ad-side clicks and platform-attributed conversions. They have no visibility into the on-site steps between landing and completion, and their attributed purchase counts are not your actual orders. They cannot localize the break either. GA4 — which could serve as a clearly-labeled `begin_checkout` proxy — is not connected to this workspace.

**What unblocks this.** Re-authorize the Shopify app with the `read_reports` scope, then confirm the shop's plan includes the Analytics reports (ShopifyQL access requires a Basic plan or higher). Once that's in place, the exact diagnostic I had queued resolves your question cleanly: the four-stage funnel for all three windows side by side, converted to stage-to-stage rates. That distinguishes the two competing explanations directly — if cart-add rate per session has fallen while checkout-reached-to-completed held steady, the break is upstream in traffic quality or landing-page relevance, and checkout is innocent. If cart-add held but checkout-reached-to-completed dropped, the break is genuinely in checkout. Traffic being up while completions are flat is fully consistent with either, which is exactly why I can't call it without the stage data.

**Short answer: partly. The keyword link holds; the user-search link does not.**

Based on Google Ads account 3202791675 (PDT Search), analysis window 2026-05-25 through 2026-06-23, I reconciled reported conversions across three layers — campaign totals, `keyword_view`, and `search_term_view`.

- **290.97 total Search conversions** reported across three enabled campaigns (21114948220, 21111476111, 21111476063). A fourth enabled campaign, Teste CPA (11503596929), had zero delivery and is not part of the reconciliation.
- **288.97 (99.3%) tie to a currently ENABLED keyword.** Every keyword carrying conversion volume returned status ENABLED — nothing traces to a paused or removed keyword.
- **Only 177.47 (61.0%) tie to a disclosed user search query.** The remaining **113.50 conversions (39.0%) are unidentifiable at the query level** — they sit on a known enabled keyword, but Google discloses no query text for them.
- **2.00 conversions (0.7%) reconcile to no keyword at all**, isolated entirely to the RS campaign (21111476111). Immaterial, but genuinely unexplained from the API.

The root cause is structural, not a tracking defect: **broad match drives 185.97 of 288.97 keyword-attributed conversions (64.4%)**, with zero exact-match conversion volume. Broad match produces a long tail of unique low-volume queries, and low-volume queries are precisely what Google suppresses from the search terms report. The evidence is in the shape of the data — 151 converting query rows, of which 126 delivered exactly one conversion each. BH (21111476063) is the weakest at 47.1% query-level loss.

There is also a second-order problem finance should know about before signing anything. Conversion counts in this account are **not whole numbers** — the two largest keywords report 70.988658 and 45.98629 conversions, and nine query rows carry fractional values including 0.994172 and several at exactly 0.5. That means some conversions are modelled rather than observed, and credit is being split fractionally across touchpoints. **Even the identified 61% is a statistical estimate with a keyword attached, not a transaction log** — so reconciling these counts to a CRM or billing record will differ by design.

Three caveats on the audit itself: the account **currency code returned UNKNOWN**, so the 19,888.01 spend figure is in unverified account currency and should be confirmed before use in any statement. Requests for network segment, ad group type, and bidding strategy were accepted but returned unpopulated, so I could not quantify how much of the query gap comes from **Search Partners placements**, where query text is systematically unavailable — this could account for a meaningful share of the 113.50 and is the first thing to check in the UI. Search-term totals were summed manually from the complete untruncated result set because the analysis sandbox was unavailable.

The full reconciliation, per-campaign gap table, and match-type breakdown are in the report above.

If useful, I can pull a keyword-to-query mapping for the three highest-spend broad keywords to show finance exactly where the disclosure ceiling falls, or check the Search Partners split directly in the UI-facing fields to close that open item.
{/final_output}

## Reconciliation — Nutripure FR (act_10150265716362407), 20–26 July 2026

**Finance should use the account-level total: 61,197.95.** It is independently corroborated by the campaign roster to the cent, and it is the only figure produced at the grain finance actually needs.

### What each source returns

```json
{"table": {"title": "Spend by Reporting Grain — 20–26 Jul 2026", "headers": ["Source", "Rows", "Spend", "Reconciles to account?"], "rows": [["Account total (level=account, no breakdown)", "1", "61,197.95", "Authoritative baseline"], ["Campaign total (level=campaign)", "17", "61,197.95", "Yes — exact match"], ["Unfiltered ad export (level=ad)", "297", "Not computed — see caveat", "No — contains orphan rows"], ["Saved Top 90 Ads by Spend", "90 of 297", "Not computed — see caveat", "No — subset by construction"]]}}
```

### Why the account and campaign totals agree

The campaign query returned 17 campaigns with `response_complete: true` and no pagination cursor. Summing those 17 values lands on **61,197.95** — identical to the account-grain figure. An exact cent-level match across two independently-computed grains is a strong validation, so both are safe for finance. Use the account row as the primary, the campaign roster as the audit trail.

### Why the ad-level totals are lower — two different causes

**The Top 90 report is a truncation, not a total.** The complete ad population for this window is 297 rows. A "Top 90 by Spend" view discards 207 of them. It is arithmetically incapable of summing to the account total and should never be used as a spend figure — it is a ranking tool. This is the single most likely source of the discrepancy you're seeing, and it is by design rather than a data fault.

**The unfiltered ad export has an integrity problem, and it does not fail cleanly in one direction.** Ad-grain exports normally run *below* campaign totals because spend from since-deleted ads still rolls up to the campaign but has no surviving ad row to attach to. However, this export also contains spend that goes the *other* way: rows 251–297 (47 rows) sit under `campaign_id 611979500009999`, named "Long-tail reconciliation remainder", with near-uniform values (3.08 spend, ~1,400 impressions, ~20 clicks each — roughly 144.66 in aggregate by hand arithmetic). I queried that campaign ID directly at campaign grain and it **returns zero rows**. Those 47 ad rows have no parent campaign in the hierarchy. Their names and uniform metrics are also inconsistent with every genuine ad in this account, which follows a strict `[NUT] - Format - Angle - Category - Product` convention.

The final page's own metadata is self-contradictory as well: it reports `response_complete: true` while simultaneously retaining the warning `"This response is incomplete at the requested reporting grain."`

### Two caveats I won't paper over

**I could not compute the exact ad-level or Top-90 totals.** The Python sandbox failed on five consecutive attempts ("Unable to connect"), and summing 297 rows by hand is not something I'll put in front of finance. I verified the campaign sum by hand only because its exact match to an independently-retrieved account figure is self-checking; the ad-level sums have no such check available. Those two cells stay blank rather than get an estimate.

**The currency is unconfirmed.** The account details endpoint returned `currency: "UNKNOWN"`. Every figure above is in the account's native currency, whatever that is. Given this is a French account the natural assumption is EUR, but I won't stamp a currency on a finance number based on an assumption — please confirm before these values enter a ledger.

### Recommended handling

Book **61,197.95** from the account grain. Keep the 17-row campaign breakdown as the supporting allocation, since it reconciles exactly and is safe for cost-centre splits. Treat both ad-level artefacts as diagnostic only, and raise the orphaned `611979500009999` rows with whoever owns the export pipeline — until they're explained, that export should not feed any financial process. Once the sandbox is back I can produce the exact ad-level and Top-90 totals and quantify the precise gap against the account figure.
{/final_output}

## Nutripure FR — Spend Reconciliation, 20–26 July 2026

Account: Nutripure FR (`act_10150265716362407`). Source: Meta Ads Insights API, fixed `time_range` 2026-07-20 → 2026-07-26.

### Which total finance should use

**Use the account-level total: 61,197.95** (account currency — see currency caveat below).

The decisive evidence is that two independently-queried grains agree to the cent. The account-level query returns a single row of 61,197.95 with no pagination involved. Summing the 17 campaign rows independently gives 61,197.95 — an exact match, which I verified by re-summing in four separate subtotal groups. An exact-to-the-cent agreement between two different query grains is not something an arithmetic slip produces, so the account figure is corroborated rather than merely asserted.

```json
{"table": {"title": "Reconciliation by Reporting Grain (20–26 Jul 2026)", "headers": ["Source", "Rows", "Spend", "Status"], "rows": [["Account level (level=account)", "1", "61,197.95", "Authoritative — use this"], ["Campaign level (level=campaign)", "17", "61,197.95", "Reconciles exactly to account"], ["Unfiltered ad export (level=ad)", "297", "Not certified — see below", "Data-quality issues found"], ["Top 90 Ads by Spend (saved report)", "90", "Structurally lower by design", "Ranked subset, not a total"]]}}
```

### Why the ad-level totals come in lower

There are three distinct causes, and they are not the same kind of problem.

**1. The Top 90 report is a ranked subset, not a total.** This is the most important point for finance. The unfiltered ad grain contains 297 ads for this window. A "Top 90 Ads by Spend" view keeps the 90 highest-spend ads and discards 207 of them. It will *always* total materially less than the account, and that gap is not an error — it is the report doing exactly what it was built to do. Using a top-N creative-analysis view as a financial control total is a category error, regardless of how the numbers look.

**2. Pagination truncation on the ad export.** The ad-level query returned 200 rows with `paging.next` present and 97 rows still outstanding. Anyone who runs this export and reads only the first response captures 200 of 297 ads and silently loses the remaining spend. This is the most common real-world cause of "the ad export doesn't tie out," and it is invisible unless you check for `paging.next`. I followed pagination to consume all 297 rows.

**3. The ad export and the campaign breakdown are not drawn from the same population.** This one is a genuine anomaly, not just a mechanical shortfall. The completed ad export contains a campaign — **"Long-tail reconciliation remainder"** (`campaign_id 611979500009999`, ads `611979500000251`–`...297`, 47 rows, roughly 144.66 of spend by hand calculation) — that **does not appear anywhere in the 17-row campaign breakdown**, even though that breakdown already sums exactly to the account total. Additionally, the final ad-level page returned contradictory quality metadata: it reported `paging_next_present: false` and "the complete 297-row ad export has been consumed" while simultaneously carrying the warning "This response is incomplete at the requested reporting grain."

Both signals point the same way: the ad grain for this window is not a clean subdivision of the account grain. Ad-level data is sound for *relative* creative comparison, but it should not be used as a financial control total for this window until that phantom campaign is explained.

### Two limitations you should know about

**I could not certify a precise sum for the 297-row ad export or the Top 90 subset.** The Python compute sandbox was unavailable — three attempts all failed with a connection error. Summing 297 values by hand and presenting the result as an exact finance-grade figure would risk introducing a fabricated-precision error into exactly the document where it does least good, so I have deliberately left those two cells uncertified rather than estimate them. The account and campaign figures are unaffected: the account total is a single API-returned value, and the campaign total is a 17-term sum I cross-checked in four groups.

**The account currency could not be verified.** `facebook_get_details_of_ad_account` returned `currency: "UNKNOWN"` for this account. Despite the "FR" in the account name, I will not assume EUR — all figures above are stated in account-currency units. Confirm the currency in Billing before these numbers go into any financial filing or cross-currency consolidation.

### Suggested next steps

Have finance book against the account-level figure with the campaign breakdown attached as supporting detail, since those two tie out exactly. Separately, the phantom campaign `611979500009999` is worth raising with whoever maintains the ad export — it is the one finding here that suggests something structurally wrong rather than merely a reporting-grain artifact. Once the compute sandbox is back I can produce the certified 297-row and Top 90 sums and issue this as a formal reconciliation report with the full variance walk.

{/final_output}

The reconciliation report is ready. Key findings:

- **Finance should book 61,197.95** for 20–26 July 2026 (account `act_10150265716362407`). The account grain and campaign grain agree at **zero variance** — and independently agree on impressions too (25,185,097 both ways), which is the strongest confirmation available.
- **The ad export paginates silently.** Page one returned 250 rows with a `paging.next` cursor still outstanding; the remaining 47 rows carry **144.66** of spend. Any ad-level pull that stops at page one is short by at least that much and gives no visual cue.
- **The Top 90 report is a subset by design** — 90 of 297 delivering ads, discarding 207. Spend per ad runs from 5,245.02 down to under 3.10 in this account, so the discarded tail is real spend, not rounding.
- **Even a complete ad export won't tie.** Some campaigns decompose exactly (Boost Com: 499.06 = 499.06 across four ads), but others fall short — CoPub influenceurs is 7.33 light, TRAFIC blog 6.47, Ebook4 3.27. Spend Meta bills to a campaign but can't pin to a live ad row never surfaces at ad grain.

Two items I'm flagging rather than smoothing over:

- The 47-row tail sits under `campaign_id 611979500009999` ("Long-tail reconciliation remainder"), a campaign that **does not appear at campaign grain at all** — and that response reported itself complete. The two grains disagree on which entities delivered. It doesn't threaten the recommended figure, but it needs explaining before any ad-grain export is used for audit.
- The account's **currency field returned UNKNOWN**. Every figure is in bare account-currency units. Confirm the billing currency from Meta Billing before posting to a ledger — the "FR" in the account name is not evidence of it.

The account and campaign totals were verified by cross-checking two independently fetched API grains on two metrics, and every conclusion above rests on that verified pair plus the exact per-campaign tests — none of it depends on the missing sums. The remaining **39.007%** is the difference between campaign-level conversions and conversions attached to disclosed search terms; the extract cannot separate privacy-threshold suppression from other Google reporting-scope differences.

The returned search-term data also did not expose the matched-keyword field despite it being requested. Consequently, the strongest defensible statement is that **177.474948 credits have identifiable query text**, not that each can be joined conclusively to one exact keyword record in this extract.

Finally, these are **fractional conversion credits**, not user-level transaction records. Google Ads aggregate reporting does not provide a unique user or conversion-event audit trail here. A true one-to-one reconciliation would require click or conversion identifiers—such as GCLID and CRM/offline-conversion records—which were not available in this dataset.

The funnel is breaking before checkout, not primarily inside checkout.

| Window | Sessions | Added to cart | Reached checkout | Completed | Overall conversion |

Versus 2025:

- Traffic rose 19.3%.
- Cart-add sessions fell 9.8%; the cart-add rate fell 24.3%.
- Checkout-reaching sessions fell 30.4%; the session-to-checkout rate fell 41.7%.
- Checkout completion among sessions reaching checkout improved from 33.0% to 35.8%.

At the 2025 overall conversion rate, current traffic would have produced about 12,919 completed checkouts—4,739 more than actual. But applying the 2025 checkout-completion rate to the checkouts actually reached would produce only about 7,536 completions, 644 fewer than the actual 8,180.

So the diagnosis is clear: higher traffic is not developing shopping intent or reaching checkout. Prioritize traffic quality, landing-page/product-page persuasion, offer alignment, and add-to-cart friction. Checkout optimization is secondary; versus 2024 its finish rate is somewhat weaker, but that decline is far smaller than the upstream collapse.

One measurement caveat: these are session-level Shopify funnel metrics, and accelerated checkout or return sessions can make stage counts non-sequential—so the reliable comparison is each stage’s incidence per session.
